newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia says political stability not threatened.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says political stability not threatened.

text.p: Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas on Wednesday sought to reassure foreign investors that the nation was politically stable and a good place to do business despite recent disturbances.

"It (the violence) does show a rather disturbing occurrence of ethnic tensions and unfortunate excesses (but) we are confident that these...are transient in nature and not reflective of a larger trend," Alatas said.

Alatas, speaking to a meeting of a number of foreign business associations, said recent outbreaks of riots and disturbances across Indonesia had been controlled by authorities and had different reasons and origins.
"Therefore, we think there should be no cause or reason for our foreign investors to see any threat to political stability," he said.

In the past few months, Indonesia has been hit by religious and ethnic disturbances in East and West Java, ethnic clashes in West Kalimantan and fighting in Central Java between supporters of rival political parties.
At least 200 people were killed in the Kalimantan violence but the other clashes were relatively minor.
Alatas said Indonesia had found from experience that the most important factors for foreign investors were political stability and consistency of economic policies.
"We as a government are determined to maintain these two particular factors," he said.
Indonesia was generally politically unstable and underdeveloped before President Suharto took power in the mid-1960s. His firm grip on power has brought about much development.

Alatas said Indonesia with its ethnically diverse population of more than 200 million spread over 6,000 islands in a 17,000 island archipelago could not afford to take political stability for granted.
"Even at a glance it is a difficult place to govern," he said.
